title: One pond, two translations
subtitle: Reading choices in Aston and Hearn
summary: Compare two historical English versions of Bashō’s poem. Locate a difference, distinguish observation from interpretation, and support a reading without declaring one final meaning.
audience: General readers; Japanese is not required.
scope: One poem and two historical English renditions. The Japanese display follows a named modern institutional transcription, not an inspected manuscript.

passages.title: Aston · 1899
passages.text:
An ancient pond!
With a sound from the water
Of the frog as it plunges in.
passages.context: Line breaks and punctuation follow the selected Academy of American Poets text.

passages.title: Hearn · selected 1914 edition
passages.text: Old pond—frogs jumping in—sound of water.
passages.context: This is one parenthetical rendition in an essay, presented here without the surrounding quotation marks/parentheses. It is not reformatted as three source lines.

passages.title: Japanese · named display witness
passages.text: 古池や蛙飛こむ水のおと
passages.context: Spelling follows the October 2, 2026 Koto City display. It is not modernized to 飛び込む or 音. No claim is made that this is a facsimile, a critical edition, or proof of every original-language reading.

claims.text: These English versions differ in how they express the frog or frogs.
claims.qualification: An English-text observation, not a finding about number in Japanese.

claims.text: Order and punctuation can invite different experiences of movement and sound.
claims.qualification: A possible reading that needs evidence; other readings can be defensible.

context: A translation is a particular writer’s rendering, not a transparent replacement for every feature of the source language.
The Japanese panel preserves a named institutional display text for context. The first task compares English; it does not automatically grade Japanese grammar or fidelity.
Hearn’s wider essay makes historical and linguistic claims that are not adopted here. This activity uses the selected rendition only.

lenses.label: Number
lenses.question: How might one pictured creature differ from a less individually focused scene?
readings: The singular can invite attention to one movement.
The plural may invite a wider scene, but does not prove simultaneous jumps.
lenses.boundary: The English wording alone cannot determine how many frogs the Japanese poem denotes.

lenses.label: Movement and sound
lenses.observation: Aston names sound before the plunging phrase; Hearn puts jumping before sound.
lenses.question: Does the order alter what you imagine noticing first?
readings: One reader may hear the event before reconstructing the movement.
Another may experience the movement and its sound as one compact event.
lenses.boundary: Reading order is observable; the reader’s imagined sequence is an interpretation.

lenses.label: Punctuation and pace
lenses.observation: The selected Aston display uses an exclamation mark and three lines; the Hearn display uses dashes without authored line breaks.
lenses.question: What pauses do you hear or imagine, and which marks support them?
readings: The exclamation can emphasize an opening perception.
The dashes can suggest cuts or connections; they do not force one emotional response.
lenses.boundary: These are features of the selected English web transcriptions. This activity does not establish the original books’ page layouts or reconstruct Bashō’s punctuation.

activity.transfer: Someone says Hearn’s plural proves that Bashō saw several frogs. Which part is observable in the English text, and which part needs evidence beyond it?
rubric: Point to exact wording in the named version.
Separate observation, possible effect and original-language claim.
Allow a different reading when it accounts for the same evidence.
